title: Golf: Precision Over Distance
summary: Why golf rewards careful, accurate shots instead of raw power, how scoring and clubs work, and why fewer strokes always wins.
poll: Hitting the ball far matters more in golf than hitting it accurately.

versions.title: Precision Over Distance
versions.text:
A player stands on a big grass field. This field is called a course. She holds a club. She swings the club. She hits a small ball. The ball must go in a hole far away. This game is golf.

Golf clubs come in many kinds. A big club can hit the ball far. A small club helps hit the ball close to the hole.

Each hit is a stroke. A player wants few strokes. The score is the count of strokes. The low score wins.

Some new kids think hitting far is best. That is not true. Hitting to the right spot is what matters most.

A good golfer plans each shot. She looks at the wind. She looks at the grass. Then she picks a club.

Golf began long ago in Scotland. Now people play golf all over the world. Some play golf in Saudi Arabia, too.

You do not need to be strong to play golf well. You need a steady hand and a good plan.

HIGH.prompt: Explain why golf rewards precision and consistency more than raw power. Include at least two supporting details and one example from the article's history or spread.

I described why accuracy saves strokes.
I mentioned a fact about golf's history or spread.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Golf rewards precision and consistency more than raw power because every single stroke counts equally toward the final score, whether it comes from a long drive or a short, careful putt. A golfer who hits the ball a long way but lands far from the hole still needs extra strokes to finish, while a golfer who controls the shot's distance and direction with an iron can save strokes and win. This emphasis on control, not strength, helps explain why golf has spread so widely since it began on the coastal terrain of Scotland, growing into a global sport played today on courses across Saudi Arabia and many other countries.
